concepts.name: Divergent Boundaries: Mechanism and Landform Outputs
key_dimensions: Seafloor spreading process and role of mantle convection currents
Landforms produced: mid-ocean ridges, rift valleys, submarine volcanoes
Continental vs. oceanic divergence (e.g., East African Rift vs. Mid-Atlantic Ridge)
UPSC trap: Divergent boundaries also occur on continents — not exclusively oceanic

concepts.name: Convergent Boundaries: Oceanic-Continental Subduction
key_dimensions: Why oceanic crust subducts under continental crust (density difference: basaltic vs. granitic)
Formation of volcanic mountain ranges, deep-sea trenches, and coastal fold mountains (e.g., Andes)
Role in generating andesitic/explosive volcanism vs. shield volcanism
UPSC trap: Subduction zone volcanoes differ in eruptive style from hotspot/rift volcanoes

concepts.name: Convergent Boundaries: Oceanic-Oceanic Subduction
key_dimensions: Formation of island arcs and associated deep-sea trenches (e.g., Mariana Trench, Japanese archipelago)
Which plate subducts when both are oceanic: the older/denser plate
Associated seismicity and tsunami generation potential
UPSC trap: Island arcs are volcanic, not fold mountains — a common confusion with collision zones

concepts.name: Convergent Boundaries: Continental-Continental Collision Zones
key_dimensions: Absence of subduction — both plates are buoyant, leading to crustal thickening and uplift
Formation of fold mountain ranges: Himalayas, Alps, Zagros
Associated features: thrust faults, nappes, deep crustal roots
UPSC trap: No volcanism at collision zones — distinguishes them from subduction convergent boundaries

concepts.name: Transform/Conservative Boundaries: Definition and Mechanism
key_dimensions: Plates slide horizontally past each other — no creation or destruction of crust
Why they are called 'conservative' boundaries
Examples: San Andreas Fault (USA), North Anatolian Fault (Turkey)
UPSC trap: Transform faults ≠ fracture zones; fracture zones are inactive remnants of transform faults

concepts.name: Mid-Ocean Ridges: Structure, Distribution and Significance
key_dimensions: Longest mountain chain on Earth (~65,000 km) — entirely submarine
Role in seafloor spreading and paleomagnetic evidence (magnetic striping)
Hydrothermal vents and unique chemosynthetic ecosystems along ridges
UPSC trap: Mid-Atlantic Ridge is slow-spreading; East Pacific Rise is fast-spreading — different morphologies

concepts.name: Seafloor Spreading and Paleomagnetic Evidence
key_dimensions: Hess's hypothesis of seafloor spreading and convection as the driving mechanism
Vine-Matthews-Morley hypothesis: symmetrical magnetic anomaly stripes as proof
Relationship between ridge-push force and plate motion
UPSC trap: Older oceanic crust is found farther from ridges and is eventually recycled — unlike continental crust

concepts.name: Subduction Zones: Wadati-Benioff Zone and Seismicity
key_dimensions: Definition: inclined plane of seismicity tracing the subducting slab into the mantle
Depth distribution of earthquakes: shallow, intermediate, and deep-focus earthquakes
Why deep-focus earthquakes (>300 km) occur only at subduction zones
UPSC trap: Deep-focus earthquakes cause less surface damage despite high magnitude — a counterintuitive fact

concepts.name: Hotspots: Distinction from Plate Boundary Volcanism
key_dimensions: Hotspots originate from mantle plumes — independent of plate boundaries
Hawaiian Islands chain as evidence of plate motion over a stationary hotspot
Hotspots can occur on both oceanic (Hawaii) and continental (Yellowstone) plates
UPSC trap: Iceland sits on both a hotspot AND a divergent boundary — a rare dual occurrence

concepts.name: Ring of Fire: Composition and Tectonic Explanation
key_dimensions: Geographic extent: ~40,000 km horseshoe around the Pacific Ocean
Accounts for ~90% of world's earthquakes and ~75% of active volcanoes
Tectonic basis: multiple convergent and transform boundaries around the Pacific Plate
UPSC trap: The Ring of Fire is NOT a single boundary — it encompasses multiple plate interactions

concepts.name: Types of Volcanoes and Their Tectonic Setting
key_dimensions: Shield volcanoes (divergent/hotspot) vs. stratovolcanoes/composite (subduction zones)
Why subduction-zone volcanoes are more explosive: silica-rich, viscous magma traps gases
Caldera formation: collapse after magma chamber evacuation vs. explosive eruption
UPSC trap: Not all volcanoes are at plate boundaries — hotspot volcanoes are intraplate

concepts.name: Earthquake Distribution and Plate Boundary Types
key_dimensions: Shallow-focus quakes: all three boundary types; deep-focus quakes: subduction zones only
Transform boundaries produce shallow but highly destructive earthquakes (e.g., 1906 San Francisco)
Intraplate earthquakes: occur away from boundaries (e.g., Koyna, Bhuj in India) — stress transfer
UPSC trap: Divergent boundaries also generate earthquakes — often overlooked in favor of convergent zones

concepts.name: Himalayan Orogeny as a Case Study of Plate Tectonics
key_dimensions: Sequence: Tethys Sea subduction → Indian Plate collision with Eurasian Plate (~50 Ma ago)
Evidence of marine fossils at high Himalayan altitudes — former Tethys Sea sediments
Continued northward movement of Indian Plate causing ongoing uplift and seismicity
UPSC trap: India moves ~5 cm/year northward — Himalayas are still rising, making them young fold mountains

concepts.name: Rift Valleys: Continental Divergence and the East African Rift System
key_dimensions: Formation by tensional forces pulling continental crust apart, creating grabens
East African Rift as a future ocean in the making — tectonic evolution stages
Associated volcanism (Mt. Kilimanjaro, Mt. Kenya) and fault-bounded lakes (Tanganyika, Malawi)
UPSC trap: Rift valleys also form at mid-ocean ridges (axial rift) — not exclusively continental

concepts.name: Tsunamis: Tectonic Origin and Triggering Mechanisms
key_dimensions: Primary cause: vertical displacement of seafloor at subduction zones (thrust earthquakes)
Why strike-slip/transform faults rarely generate tsunamis (horizontal, not vertical displacement)
2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami: Sumatra-Andaman subduction zone — megathrust earthquake
UPSC trap: Tsunami speed, wavelength, and amplitude behavior in deep vs. shallow water — a common MCQ angle

concepts.name: Wilson Cycle: Complete Lifecycle of an Ocean Basin
key_dimensions: Six stages: embryonic (rift) → juvenile (narrow sea) → mature (wide ocean) → declining → terminal → suturing
East African Rift = embryonic; Atlantic = mature; Himalayas = sutured remnant of Tethys
Explains repetitive opening and closing of ocean basins over geological time
UPSC trap: The Wilson Cycle integrates all boundary types into a single temporal framework — often tested as an integrative concept

concepts.name: Driving Forces of Plate Motion: Ridge Push vs. Slab Pull
key_dimensions: Ridge push: elevated mid-ocean ridges create gravitational sliding force on plates
Slab pull: subducting dense oceanic crust pulls the rest of the plate — considered the dominant force
Role of mantle convection: now debated as a consequence of, not cause of, plate motion
UPSC trap: Slab pull is stronger than ridge push — counterintuitive to the traditional convection-only explanation

concepts.name: Accretionary Prisms and Forearc/Backarc Basins at Subduction Zones
key_dimensions: Accretionary prism: scraped-off sediments from subducting plate piling up at the trench
Forearc basin: between accretionary prism and volcanic arc — sediment trap
Backarc basin: extensional tectonics behind volcanic arc, can form small spreading centers
UPSC trap: Backarc basins show divergent features (spreading) within a convergent tectonic setting — a conceptual trap

concepts.name: Fracture Zones vs. Transform Faults: A Critical Distinction
key_dimensions: Transform fault: active portion between two offset ridge segments — plates moving in opposite directions
Fracture zone: inactive extension beyond ridge segments — plates moving in same direction, no relative motion
Seismic activity confined to transform fault segment only, not the fracture zone
UPSC trap: On maps, both look like linear features cutting across ridges — only the segment between ridges is seismically active

concepts.name: Terrane Accretion and Exotic Terranes
key_dimensions: Terranes: fragments of crustal material with distinct geological history accreted onto a larger plate
Role in building continental margins (e.g., western North America, parts of the Tibetan Plateau)
Distinction from normal plate collision: terranes are smaller, buoyant blocks that do not subduct
UPSC trap: Much of the Tibetan Plateau and parts of the Himalayas are composed of accreted terranes — not purely Indian Plate material
